title: Sign of a Number
directAnswer: Compare `n` with 0: greater → 1, less → -1, equal → 0. Order the checks so zero is handled correctly.

remember.takeaway: Whenever a value splits into 3 outcomes, write 3 guarded returns.
remember.formula: if n>0 return 1; if n<0 return -1; return 0;

problemStatement: Given an integer `n`, return `1` if it is positive, `-1` if negative, and `0` if it is zero.
understanding: Three-way branch on the value's relationship to zero.

approaches.name: Three-way comparison
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
There are exactly three outcomes — positive, negative, zero — so the cleanest solution is three guarded returns: `if (n > 0) return 1; if (n < 0) return -1; return 0;`.

**Why guarded returns beat one big if/else.** Each `return` exits immediately, so the branches are automatically mutually exclusive and you can't accidentally fall into two of them. The final `return 0` is reached only when both comparisons failed, which is precisely the `n == 0` case — so you never even write `== 0` explicitly.

**Why order is flexible but coverage is not.** You may test `< 0` first or `> 0` first; what matters is that all three cases are covered and zero has a home. The classic bug is forgetting zero and returning a wrong default.

**Library shortcut.** `Integer.signum(n)` (Java) or `(n > 0) - (n < 0)` (a branchless C-style trick) both do this; mention them but show the explicit logic when fundamentals are being tested.
hints: How many distinct outcomes are there? Map each to a return value.
Three guarded returns make the cases mutually exclusive for free.
The fall-through `return 0` handles zero without an explicit `== 0` test.

dryRun.intro: Guarded returns, checked top to bottom.

edgeCases.behavior: Both comparisons fail, so the function falls through to `return 0`.
Returns 1; no arithmetic is done so there's no overflow risk.

pitfalls: Forgetting the zero case and returning a stray default.
Using overlapping conditions so a value could match two branches.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the zero case and returning a wrong default.
Using `Integer.signum`/`math.copysign` when asked to show the logic.
patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Three-way branch. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.
